skills.name: design-taste-frontend
skills.description: tasteskill v2, the anti-slop frontend skill. Art direction for websites, distilled from a study of 247 curated gallery sites (One Page Love, Awwwards Sites of the Day). Deals researched directions (idea, composition, type, palette, photographs, section blueprints) from a library, enforces a strict no-slop house style with a real-browser inspector, and runs a look-and-fix loop on screenshots. Use this whenever you build, design, redesign, restyle, polish or review a landing page, marketing site, portfolio, product page, one-pager, hero or any public-facing web page, in any stack (HTML/CSS, React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Tailwind) — also when the user says a page looks generic, templated, "AI-made", sloppy, or asks to make it look designed, premium, award-level or less like every other site. Not for dashboards or app screens.

references/colour.md.text:
# Colour

The direction sheet deals a palette with named roles. This file is how to apply it so the page looks
decided rather than tinted.

## Contents

1. What the study measured
2. The roles
3. Proportion
4. Surfaces without lines or shadows
5. Colour fields
6. Dark pages
7. Colour and photographs
8. Contrast
9. Banned families, and what "warm" means here

## 1. What the study measured

- 41% of the studied pages are dark, 59% light. A quarter sit on pure white; 12% on pure black.
- Schemes, as the panel classed them: monochrome plus one accent 23%, light neutral 22%, dark neutral
  14%, several flat colours 13%, strictly two-tone 12%, colour carried by photographs 9%, one saturated
  field 6%.
- Buttons are neutral (black, white, grey) on 52% of sites. A coloured button is a choice, not a
  requirement.
- Gradient fills appear on 22% of the top-scored sites and 52% of the weak ones; gradient text on 2%
  against 13%.
- One site in 246 has a terracotta primary button and none has a violet one. Those are colours of
  generated pages, not of the gallery. Warm off-white grounds do occur (32 sites), nearly always with
  a dark or green ink rather than an orange accent.
- Top-scored sites change the page's field colour between sections more often (a median of two section
  grounds against one).

## 2. The roles

```css
:root {
  --bg: …;          /* the ground: most of the surface */
  --surface: …;     /* one tone step from the ground: filled panels, form fields, tiles */
  --ink: …;         /* main text and the strongest marks */
  --muted: …;       /* secondary text; still passes contrast on --bg */
  --accent: …;      /* the one accent */
  --accent-ink: …;  /* text on the accent */
  /* --field-1 … --field-n and their inks, when the palette has section fields */
}
```

Use the tokens for every colour in the build. A raw hex in a component is a second palette starting.
Do not add greys between the roles: if you need a quieter text, it is `--muted`; if you need a quieter
surface, it is `--surface`.

## 3. Proportion

Decide the shares before colouring anything and check them in the screenshot:

- **Ground:** 70–90% of the page.
- **Ink:** text and perhaps one inverted section (ink as ground, ground as ink).
- **Accent:** under 5% of any screen. It marks the action and at most one other recurring thing. The
  moment it appears in five places it stops meaning "here".

Palettes with fields (flat-loud, pastel) work differently: each section is one field at full strength
and the proportion rule applies inside each section (field, its ink, nothing else).

The accent is not for headings, icons, bullets, borders or underlines unless the direction sheet says
so. A headline is ink.

## 4. Surfaces without lines or shadows

With rules and shadows banned, a surface is told apart from the ground by tone alone:

```css
.panel { background: var(--surface); }          /* 2–6 lightness points from --bg */
.field { background: var(--surface); border: 0; } /* inputs: filled, with a clear focus state */
.field:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }
```

- One step is enough. If a panel does not read, increase padding or separate with space before
  reaching for a second tone.
- Do not nest a panel inside a panel.
- Images do not need a frame. If a light photograph melts into a light ground, change the crop or set
  it on `--surface`, do not outline it.
- A thick bar (4px or more) in ink or accent is a graphic element, allowed where the direction uses
  it. A 1px line is not.

## 5. Colour fields

A section that changes the whole ground colour is the strongest colour move available, and it replaces
dividers, cards and background decoration at once.

- Fields meet edge to edge with a hard line. Nothing fades.
- Every field has its own assigned ink from the palette. Never put `--muted` on a coloured field; use
  the field's ink at full strength, or at 70% opacity for secondary text if it still passes contrast.
- Neighbouring fields should differ in lightness, not only in hue, or the page vibrates.
- Order them like chapters: open strong, rest, surprise, close dark or very light.
- The page's meta theme colour and the navigation follow the first field.

## 6. Dark pages

- Put `color-scheme: dark` on the root so form controls and scrollbars follow.
- The ground is a deep tone with a slight tint from the palette, and the ink is a soft light, not
  `#fff` on `#000`, unless the palette deals exactly that for a stark two-tone direction.
- Secondary text is where dark pages fail: check `--muted` against the ground (4.5:1).
- Depth on dark comes from a lighter surface step, never from glows or coloured light.
- Use lighter font weights than you would on a light page.

## 7. Colour and photographs

- When photographs carry the colour, the interface stays neutral and takes its ink from the darkest
  tone in the imagery.
- Do not wash a photograph with the brand colour. Either leave it alone, or commit to a real treatment
  for every image on the page (all greyscale, or all untouched).
- Text over a photograph needs a calm region. If there is none, move the text off the image. A neutral
  scrim (black or the ink colour, 30–55% opacity, flat or fading over the text area only) is the one
  gradient the inspector allows.
- A flat field sampled from a photograph (its sky, its shadow) makes a section sit with that image.

## 8. Contrast

- Body text 4.5:1 or better; display type and large numerals 3:1 or better; the dealt palettes meet
  7:1 for ink on ground.
- `inspect.mjs` computes contrast for text on flat grounds and fails anything under 2.6:1. It cannot
  see text over photographs: check those in the screenshots yourself.
- Do not lower opacity on text to make it "soft" unless you have checked the resulting ratio.
- Focus states and hover states increase contrast, never reduce it.

## 9. Banned families, and what "warm" means here

The inspector fails these:

- **Cream with terracotta.** A yellow-cream ground (roughly hue 22–62, light and noticeably
  saturated) with a rust, clay or burnt-orange accent is the house look of AI assistants and of the
  pages they generate. Either half alone is suspect; together they are unmistakable.
- **Violet and indigo.** The first wave of generated pages was purple; it still reads that way.

If the brief wants warmth, get it from a low-chroma stone, bone or putty ground (saturation under
about 15%), from a deep green, brown or oxblood ink, from photographs, or from a full warm field
(mustard, tomato red, pink) used flat and with conviction. Warmth is not beige.

If the brand itself owns one of the banned colours, it is the brand's and you keep it: use
`--keep palette`, pass `--allow palette-purple` (or the relevant rule) to the inspector, and note it in
the report.

# Words Copy is the first design decision. A headline that needs four lines cannot be rescued by typography, and a page of slogans cannot be rescued by layout. Write the page as plain text before any markup. ## Contents 1. Write the argument first 2. The two-line headline (with the character budget) 3. Headline shapes that work 4. Supporting line, body, buttons 5. Proof without inventing it 6. Things that read as generated 7. Micro-typography ## 1. Write the argument first Answer in one line each, in a scratch note: - Who is reading, and what do they already know? - What is this, said the way its maker would say it to a friend? - What single thing should the reader believe after one screen? - What would make them believe it (a picture of the thing, a number, a name, a demonstration)? - What do they do next? Then list the page as claims, one per section, each with its proof: ``` 1. It is a three-legged oak stool, made to order. → the stool, large 2. Each seat is cut from one board, so the grain is yours. → three close-ups 3. It takes six weeks, and you can follow it. → the stages, photographed 4. It costs 240 and is delivered by the maker. → price, button ``` A section with no claim is filler; delete it. This is also how you escape the stock order of hero, logos, features, testimonial, pricing, call to action: the order of the argument is the order of the page. ## 2. The two-line headline A headline is a title. It is held in one glance. On the studied gallery sites the hero headline has a median of 5 words and 70% sit on one or two lines at desktop width. Every headline on your page, at every viewport, fits in **two lines or fewer**. `inspect.mjs` measures this at 1440, 768 and 390 pixels and fails the page otherwise. The constraint is arithmetic, so do it before you fall in love with a sentence: ``` characters per line ≈ line width in px ÷ (font size in px × k) k ≈ 0.40 condensed faces k ≈ 0.50 most grotesks and serifs at display size, tight tracking k ≈ 0.58 wide / extended faces, all-caps settings ``` | Where | Line width | Size | Per line | Two-line budget | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Phone 390, 20px gutters | 350px | 44px | ~16 | **~32 characters** | | Phone 390, 20px gutters | 350px | 34px | ~21 | ~42 characters | | Tablet 768 | 690px | 64px | ~22 | ~44 characters | | Desktop, 12-col measure | 1100px | 104px | ~21 | ~42 characters | | Desktop, half width | 620px | 72px | ~17 | ~34 characters | So a hero headline of **about 32 characters or fewer** (four to six words) survives everywhere at a confident size. Up to about 42 works if the phone size comes down to the mid-30s. Past that you are writing a sentence; move the rest into the supporting line. Controlling the break: - Give the headline a `max-width` in `ch` so it breaks where you intend, and add `text-wrap: balance` so two lines come out even. - Where the break matters (it usually does), author it: `Stools for
small kitchens`. Check the phone screenshot; if an authored line wraps there, hide the `
` under a breakpoint or shorten. - Never fix a long headline only by shrinking it. A timid 28px headline of nine words is worse than five words at 64px. - Avoid a single orphan word on line two. Rebalance by cutting a word, not by nudging the width. Section headings follow the same rule and are shorter: two to five words. **A statement is not a headline.** An intro sentence or a quotation set large (the manifesto line after the hero, a testimonial) is a paragraph: mark it up as `

` or `

`, keep it to about 25 words, and set it at statement size, which the inspector takes as 36px or less on desktop, 32px on a tablet and 24px on a phone. It may then run to about three lines (four on a phone). Set larger than that, or marked up as a heading, or placed as the main line of the first screen, it is a headline and gets two lines. In blind judging, a sentence set big over three or more lines was read as a long headline every time, whatever its markup; if the words matter that much, cut them to a two-line headline instead. ## 3. Headline shapes that work All seen repeatedly on the gallery sites. Pick the plainest one that is true. - **The name.** The brand or the person, set very large, with a one-line description elsewhere. Strongest when the name is short and the subject is visual (studios, restaurants, hotels, people). - **What it is.** "A vinyl shelf in your pocket." "Furniture for small rooms." Category, stated with one specific word. - **The claim.** "Your bank won't do this." One sentence a competitor could not sign. - **The instruction.** "Understand your money." Verb first, short. - **The place or the moment.** "Antarctica." "Lisbon, since 1984." For hospitality, events, travel. Shapes to avoid, because they are the average of every landing page: - The mad-lib: "The AI-powered platform for modern teams". - The tricolon: "Fast. Simple. Secure." or "Plan. Build. Ship." - The correction: "It's not just a tool, it's a workflow". Also "More than a …". - "X, reimagined / redefined / made simple". "Welcome to …". "Meet …" for a product nobody has met. - A question the reader did not ask. - A headline that needs its colon: "Ledgerly: invoicing for freelancers". Drop the name, it is in the navigation. - One word of the headline styled differently (italic, serif, coloured, underlined, in a pill). Sentence case. No full stop unless the direction's voice uses them everywhere. ## 4. Supporting line, body, buttons **Supporting line.** One sentence, at most about 22 words, that says concretely what the thing is and who it is for. It is where the detail cut from the headline goes. It never repeats the headline in other words. **Body.** Short paragraphs of plain statements. Prefer the specific noun and the real number: "ships in a week" over "fast delivery"; "38 seats" over "intimate". Read every sentence and ask whether a different company could print it unchanged; if so, sharpen it or cut it. **Buttons.** Name the action or the thing: "Book a table", "See the plans", "Download for Mac". One to three words. The primary action keeps one name everywhere on the page. One primary button per screen; a second action is a plain text link. No arrow glyph on every link and button; at most one arrow, on the primary action, if the direction uses arrows at all. **Navigation.** The wordmark, up to five plain links, one action. Link labels are single nouns. ## 5. Proof without inventing it Never invent customers, quotes from named people, press logos, user counts, ratings or benchmarks. Invented proof is both dishonest and a recognised tell. When the brief supplies no proof, use what is true by construction: - Show the thing itself, large. A real demonstration outranks any quote. - State how it works, specifically. - Use facts from the brief (price, place, year, materials, what is included). - If a testimonial or logo section is explicitly requested and no real ones exist, build the section with plainly fictional sample content and say so in your final report so it is replaced before launch. Do not put real company names or real people in it. **Sample details are different from proof, and they are expected.** Where the brief gives the shape of the content but not every detail (six rooms "from €140", "a short menu", twelve speakers), write the full set of plausible details: each room with a name, a bed, a view and its own rate; each dish with its price; each speaker with a talk title. A design can only be judged at its real density, and a page that shows one rate where six rooms exist looks unfinished. List every sample detail in the report so the client confirms or replaces it. ## 6. Things that read as generated `lint.mjs` flags most of these. - Verbs and adjectives of the genre: unlock, unleash, supercharge, elevate, empower, streamline, seamless, effortless, robust, cutting-edge, next-generation, world-class, all-in-one, blazing fast. - Labels pretending to be editorial: "Field notes", "The details", "Our philosophy", "Quietly trusted by". A section heading can simply be "Pricing". - Furniture text: locale or time strips, "Est. 2024", coordinates, version stamps, "Scroll", "(Scroll to explore)", fake photo credits, status lines such as "Available for work" with a dot, strings of words separated by middle dots or slashes. - The em dash as a habit. One or two on a page read as writing; ten read as a model. Use a full stop. - Explainer captions that narrate the design: "A clean, minimal layout for…". - Step labels that duplicate numbers: "Step 1", "Phase 02". - Three parallel items everywhere: three features, three stats, three steps. Use the number the content has. ## 7. Micro-typography - Curly quotes and apostrophes (“ ” ’), a real ellipsis (…), an en dash for ranges (9–5). - Non-breaking space between a number and its unit, and before the last short word of a headline when it would otherwise orphan (` `). - `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` where numbers line up in columns (prices, tables). - `text-wrap: balance` on headings, `text-wrap: pretty` on paragraphs. - No all-caps for anything longer than three words; if you set caps, add 0.02–0.06em tracking. - No text under 13px. No centred paragraphs longer than three lines. No justified text.

references/critique.md.text:
# Critique — judging the render

`inspect.mjs` passing means nothing banned or broken was measured. It says nothing about whether the
page is good. This file is how you find out. Use it on the screenshots, never on the code: you wrote
the code, so you will read your intentions into it. The pictures only show what is there.

## Contents

1. How to look (fourteen passes, a few minutes)
2. The score
3. Caps
4. Writing the critique
5. What to fix first
6. When to stop

## 1. How to look

Open `desktop-fold.jpg`, then the `desktop-page-*.jpg` sheets, then `mobile-fold.jpg` and the mobile
sheets. Make each pass on its own; do not blend them.

1. **One second.** Glance and look away. What did you see? There should be exactly one answer: a
   word, an image, an object. If the answer is "a website", there is no focal point.
2. **Squint.** Blur your attention until text becomes grey bars. The page should reduce to two or
   three large masses with clear size differences. Many small similar masses means everything is
   medium and nothing leads.
3. **Cover the logo.** Could this first screen belong to a competitor, or to a different industry?
   If swapping the name and the noun in the headline would produce an equally valid page, the page has
   no idea. Go back to the direction sheet; the idea is written there. Then scroll: does the idea reach
   the pricing, the FAQ and the footer, or does the page turn into stock blocks after the first screen?
4. **Edges.** Follow the left edge of every text block down the page. Count the distinct x positions.
   A composed page has two or three, reused on purpose. Six means things were placed one at a time.
5. **Space.** Are related things close and unrelated things far? Is the gap between sections clearly
   larger than any gap inside a section? Is any region empty by accident (a hole) rather than by
   decision (a rest)? A hole usually sits beside a short column or under a removed decoration.
6. **Type.** Is the jump from body text to headline decisive (three times or more)? Do you see more
   than five sizes? Any headline with one orphan word on its last line? Any paragraph wider than about
   75 characters or centred over more than three lines?
7. **Colour.** Name the proportions: which colour holds most of the surface, which supports, where is
   the accent? An accent that appears in ten places means nothing. One that appears on the single
   action and one detail means "here".
8. **Images.** Count the real pictures: are there at least four, and is there a moving one? A page of
   drawings only, or of type only, looks unfinished next to one with real photographs and footage.
   Is every image doing a job (showing the thing, setting the place, proving the claim)?
   Do the crops share ratios? Is anything a grey box, a stretched photo, a fake screen made of bars?
   Does the photography share one light and one grade, or is it a stock mix?
9. **Sameness.** Write one word for each section's layout (split, list, full-bleed, grid, statement,
   index …). The same word twice in a row, or three times on the page, is the template showing.
10. **Phone.** Is the mobile screen a composition of its own, with its own crop and its own line
    breaks, or the desktop page squeezed? Is the first screen still one clear thing?
11. **Fullness.** Go through the desktop sheets screen by screen. Is each screen a composed poster, or
    is it a narrow column of small text with dead ground either side? Is any statement held on screen
    for three screens? An austere page is not a restrained one: if the page could be mistaken for an
    unfinished wireframe (grey shapes, grey text, one small column), it is underbuilt. A single motif or
    drawing blown up to fill a whole screen with nothing to read is a hole too, however bold it looks.
12. **Substance.** Does every section the brief asked for deliver its information completely and at a
    readable size (the full menu, each room, every speaker, the price and what it includes)? Would the
    visitor leave knowing what they came to find out? Is the primary action a real button on the first
    screen?
13. **Collisions.** Is anything lying on top of a headline, a statement or a button at any scroll
    position? Does any element run off the edge of the phone screen? A row that scrolls sideways on
    the phone reads as cut off in a screenshot and to most visitors; wrap it unless the cut is
    plainly deliberate (a partial card showing at the edge).
14. **The competitor and the live thing.** Put the nearest competitor's name on the page: does the
    idea still work? Then name the one live thing (what the visitor can do or what differs each visit).
    If either answer is weak, that is the first problem of the round, ahead of any detail.

A note from testing: in blind comparisons a richer page full of template devices beat a cleaner page
that was thin, every time. The house rules remove the devices; passes 11–13 are where you make sure the
page did not lose its substance with them.

## 2. The score

Score like an Awwwards juror: four criteria, 1–10 each, weighted **design 40%, usability 30%,
creativity 20%, content 10%**.

**Design (40%)** — composition, typography, colour, imagery, craft.
- 9–10: every screen holds as a poster. Nothing could be removed or moved.
- 8: confident and coherent; one or two soft spots a designer would notice.
- 7: clean and professional, a clear system, little tension.
- 6: tidy but anonymous. Reads as a kit.
- 5 or less: weak hierarchy, accidental spacing, default type, mismatched images.

**Usability (30%)** — orientation in three seconds, readable text, obvious actions, honest mobile.
- 9–10: you know what it is, who it is for and what to do without scrolling; flawless on a phone.
- 8: clear and comfortable; minor friction (a long section, a small target).
- 7: works, with one real problem (weak contrast somewhere, a cramped phone layout).
- 6 or less: you have to hunt, or something breaks.

**Creativity (20%)** — an idea you can state in a sentence, carried through.
- 9–10: a concept specific to this subject that you have not seen applied this way.
- 8: a clear idea with one memorable move.
- 7: a tasteful execution of a known approach.
- 6 or less: the category default.

**Content (10%)** — words and pictures that are specific, true-sounding and edited.
- 9–10: every line could only be about this subject; imagery is the subject.
- 7–8: clear and concrete, some generic lines.
- 6 or less: slogans, filler, stock.

`overall = 0.4·design + 0.3·usability + 0.2·creativity + 0.1·content`

For calibration: real Sites of the Day land around 7.5–8.0 overall from the jury. An honest 8.5 is
rare. If your first score for your own work is 9, score it again as the juror who did not build it.

## 3. Caps

These override the arithmetic.

- Any `FAIL` still reported by `inspect.mjs`: overall cannot exceed **6.0**.
- A headline of three or more lines at any viewport, an eyebrow label, monospace labels, 01/02/03
  numbering, a decorative gradient, a shadow on a resting element, or a decorative hairline visible in
  a screenshot: overall cannot exceed **6.5**, whatever else is true.
- Pass 3 fails (the page could belong to anyone): creativity cannot exceed **6**.
- The idea passes for the nearest competitor (pass 14): creativity cannot exceed **7**.
- Fewer than four real pictures (photographs, archival images, footage; drawings do not count):
  design cannot exceed **6.5**.
- A page that barely moves (the inspector's `still-page`), or motion that is one identical fade on
  every block: design cannot exceed **7**.
- No live thing (pass 14): creativity cannot exceed **7.5**.
- Any placeholder (grey box, lorem, "Image here"): content cannot exceed **5**.
- Two or more desktop screens that are mostly empty ground, or a page whose running text is small and
  grey: design cannot exceed **6.5**.
- A section the brief asked for that is missing or reduced to a few words: content cannot exceed **6**.
- No real button for the primary action on the first screen: usability cannot exceed **7**.
- Anything covering a headline at any scroll position: usability cannot exceed **6**.
- A blank band where a reveal did not fire, or content clipped off-screen: usability cannot exceed **5**.

## 4. Writing the critique

Write it down; do not just think it. Use exactly this shape so rounds can be compared:

```
ROUND n
Seen in one second: …
Idea (one sentence): …
Live thing: …
Layout words by section: hero=… / …=… / …
Scores: design _ · usability _ · creativity _ · content _ → overall _._
Caps applied: …
Top three problems (most visible first), each with the screenshot it shows in and the fix:
1. …
2. …
3. …
```

Name problems the way a designer would to a colleague: "the supporting paragraph starts 40px left of
the headline's edge", "the testimonial section is the third split layout in a row", "the phone hero
crops the bottle out of frame". "Could be more polished" is not a finding.

## 5. What to fix first

Fix in this order; later items cannot rescue earlier ones.

1. **The idea.** If pass 3 fails, change the hero concept, not the details.
2. **Hierarchy.** One dominant element per screen. Make the big thing bigger and the small things
   fewer before touching anything else.
3. **Composition.** Shared edges, section spacing, variety of layout between sections, holes.
4. **Typography.** Scale contrast, line breaks, measure, leading.
5. **Imagery.** Replace weak pictures, unify crops and grade.
6. **Colour.** Proportion and accent discipline.
7. **Detail.** States, focus, small alignments, mobile refinements.
8. **Motion.** Last.

When removing something leaves a gap, do not refill it with an ornament. Close the gap, enlarge what
remains, or let a picture or a colour field take the space.

## 6. When to stop

Run at most three rounds: critique → fix the top three → re-inspect → critique. Stop early when a round
finds no problem a stranger would notice. If round three still scores under 7.5, say so plainly in
your report, with the remaining problems listed; do not round up.

references/imagery.md.text:
# Imagery Pictures are where generated pages most obviously give up: a grey box, an icon in a square, a fake dashboard, an abstract blob. This file is how to decide what the pictures are, where to find real ones, how to crop and place them, and what to do when there are none. ## Contents 1. What the study measured 2. Decide what imagery exists 3. Real pictures from the open collections 4. The dealt photographs 5. Cropping and placing 6. Treatment 7. Showing software 8. Drawing the subject 9. Type and colour alone 10. Markup and credits 11. Video ## 1. What the study measured - On 60% of the studied sites one piece of media covers at least half of the first screen; on half of them it covers nearly all of it. Top-scored sites: 68% and 56%. Weak sites: 48% and 39%. - Only 15% of heroes have no media at all, and those are deliberate typographic statements. - Media has square corners on 73% of sites. Where corners are rounded the usual radius is about 12px, applied to every image alike. - Top-scored pages carry far more imagery (a median of 37 images against 5 on weak pages): the strong sites show, the weak ones tell. - What the imagery is, by the panel's classification: a mix of kinds 32%, photography 14%, generative or WebGL scenes 13%, real product interface 12%, 3D renders 11%, illustration 9%, video 6%, type only 3%. - Among the 54 sites the panel scored under 6.8, legibility (text lost over a busy image, or too little contrast) was named as a weakness in 13. ## 2. Decide what imagery exists In order of preference: 1. **The project's own images.** Product shots, the place, the people, the work. Even ordinary photographs of the real thing beat beautiful photographs of something else. Ask what exists; look in the repository. 2. **Images you can generate** with an image tool in this session. Write prompts as a photographer's brief: subject, angle, light, background, crop ratio, and "no text". Generate the hero first and make the rest match its light. 3. **Real pictures of the subject's world from the open collections** (section 3). Archives, museums and photographers have published millions of pictures anyone may use with a credit: the client's city and street in old postcards, maps of its neighbourhood, its materials, its trade in engravings, museum objects of its kind. Whenever an honest one exists, it beats a drawing of the same thing: it is real, it has detail no drawing in a page's budget reaches, and it carries history. Honest means nobody could take it for the client's own product, room, dish, person or team. 4. **Pictures you draw in code from the subject itself** (section 8), for what no honest picture exists of: the product's own objects as flat shapes, the place's tiles and windows, a map of its streets, the document a tool produces, the interface of a piece of software. In testing, pages that drew their subject with care beat pages that borrowed unrelated photographs every time, and beat pages that showed nothing. 5. **The photographs dealt on the direction sheet.** Real photographs of places, light, texture and weather. Use them only where an honestly generic picture fits (the open sea for a house on the sea, fog for a quiet retreat). They cannot stand in for a specific product, dish, room, person or screen: a foggy motorway on a restaurant page reads as stock at once, and jurors notice. 6. **Type and colour alone,** done on purpose (section 9). Tell `draw.mjs` the truth with `--have`. If you have no product photographs and no image tool, do not pass `product-photo`; the draw will avoid the directions that depend on showing the object. Pictures found in the open collections are not the project's own: do not pass `photography` for them. ## 3. Real pictures from the open collections `scripts/assets.mjs` searches four open sources without keys and prints, for each find, a direct image URL, the page it comes from, its size, its creator, its licence and a credit line: - **Openverse**: one index over Flickr, Wikimedia Commons, museums and libraries. - **Wikimedia Commons**: archival photographs, old maps, scans of prints and books, places as they look now. - **The Art Institute of Chicago** and **The Metropolitan Museum of Art**: public-domain paintings, prints, drawings, photographs, textiles and objects, in large scans. ```bash node /scripts/assets.mjs "ghent postcard" node /scripts/assets.mjs "fig" --source museums --orientation portrait node /scripts/assets.mjs "basalt texture" --min-width 2400 --source openverse,commons node /scripts/assets.mjs --get commons:36649959,met:707892 # download, record the credits node /scripts/assets.mjs --credits # footer line and report list ``` By default it keeps only licences that allow commercial use (CC0, public domain, CC BY, CC BY-SA) and pictures at least 1000 pixels wide, and checks that every image it prints actually loads. `--license pd` keeps only pictures that need no credit; `--orientation`, `--min-width` and `--limit` narrow the list; `--source` picks the sources; `--json` gives the raw results. Each result has a ref (`commons:36649959`) that `--get` takes. **What to search for.** The inventory (SKILL.md step 1), not the category: "bakery" finds other people's bakeries. The subject's world is specific: - **Its place:** the city, the street, the harbour, the valley, in old postcards and photographs ("ghent postcard", "rotterdam harbour 1920") and as it looks today ("gent korenmarkt"). - **Its maps:** the street plan, the chart of its bay, the geology of its valley ("ghent old map", "nautical chart lisbon"). - **Its materials,** close enough to read as a surface: the stone of its quay, the grain of its oak, its glaze, its tiles ("azulejo tiles", "basalt cobblestones", "oak grain"). - **Its trade's history:** the old tools, the craft in engravings and trade catalogues, patent drawings ("bread oven engraving", "potter's wheel", "bicycle patent drawing"). - **Museum objects of its kind,** with `--source museums`: a coffee set from about 1810 for a studio that makes coffee sets, a woodblock print of a wave for a surf school, a porcelain plate painted with figs for a fig orchard. - **Scientific imagery:** botanical and zoological plates ("botanical engraving fig"), star charts, microscope photographs, satellite views of its coast, geological sections. Search in the place's own words (azulejo, not "blue tile"; Korenmarkt, not "market square"), add a medium (postcard, engraving, old map, lithograph, aerial photograph) or a decade, and try two or three queries per idea. The museum sources match best on one or two words ("fig", "harbour", "teapot"). **What makes a good find.** - It belongs to this subject's world and would not fit the nearest competitor's page. - It still reads at the crop the slot needs. Look at it before deciding: `--get` downloads it, then open the file. A title is not a picture. - It is large enough: twice the width it is shown at for anything full-bleed (the script prints the largest size available). A 1024-pixel Flickr photograph is a half-width picture at most. - It belongs to one family with the others on the page: all engravings, or all photographs from one era, or all close surfaces in one light. A 1900 postcard beside a modern stock photograph beside a botanical plate reads as a scrapbook. - No watermark, no burned-in text or logo, no frame or scanner edge you cannot crop away, and no recognisable living person who could be taken for the client's staff or customers. **Use it creatively.** Found pictures are material, not decoration: - **One archival photograph as the hero,** full-bleed: the street as it was a century ago, behind the name of the business that stands in it today, with the year in the caption. - **A museum engraving enlarged until its line becomes texture,** cropped tight and returning at different scales as the page's one motif (the whole fig plate in the hero, a single leaf of it beside the menu). - **An engraving or a map on white paper set with `mix-blend-mode: multiply` on the page's colour field,** so the ink sits on the ground (section 6). - **The real map of the street as the contact section,** the door marked, the north and the scale taken from the original. - **A material close-up as a whole field:** the quay's stone behind the opening hours. - **A run of old postcards or plates as the gallery,** one size, one treatment. Treatments stay within section 6: untouched, greyscale for the whole set, or multiply on a field. **Stay honest.** - **A found picture is never the client's own.** It may show the client's city, its materials, its history, the kind of thing it makes; it may never stand in for the client's product, room, dish, person, team or customers. If a visitor could take it for the client's own (a bakery counter, a plate of pasta, a smiling barista, a guest room), do not use it. - **Caption from the source** when a caption helps: what it is and when, as the archive describes it ("Gand, unloading a steamer, 1905"). Never write a caption that ties it to the client. - **Record and credit every picture.** `--get` writes the source, creator, licence and page of each download to `assets/credits.json`. CC BY and CC BY-SA require a credit with the title, the creator, a link to the source and a link to the licence; `--credits` prints them as one line of HTML for the footer (section 10). Public-domain pictures need no credit; give one anyway. - **Respect the licence.** CC BY-SA: an altered version (recoloured, combined with other pictures) must be shared under the same licence. Non-commercial (NC) and no-derivatives (ND) licences are out for a client's site, which is why the script leaves them out unless asked. Read the `note` lines: some pictures carry personality rights or a trademark, are public domain only in the United States, or come with an archive's statement instead of a licence. - **Download, do not hotlink.** Save what you use into the project: `--get` puts it in `assets/` at 1920 pixels wide (pass `--width 1280` for a picture shown at half the screen, `--width 3840` for a very large hero where the source has it). The page then works offline, does not break when an archive moves a file, and does not load from someone else's server. Every licence the script allows by default permits copying. - **List them in the report:** file, title, creator, licence, source page, and where the credit sits. `--credits` prints that list too. If two or three honest queries per idea find nothing that fits, draw (section 8). A drawing made for the subject is better than a found picture that is merely nearby. If the script cannot reach any source (no network), draw, and say so in the report. For moving pictures, the same script searches real footage with `--video` (section 11). ## 4. The dealt photographs - The sheet lists eight from one set so they share a subject and a light. Use three to six. - Each line says where the calm area is. Put text there or keep text off the image. - More from the same or another set: `node scripts/draw.mjs --photos list`, `--photos `, or `--photos "fog coast"` to search descriptions. - URLs have the form `https://picsum.photos/id///`. Request the exact pixel size you render at twice the CSS size for sharpness, capped around 2400 wide. Add `?grayscale` for black-and-white. - These are photographs from Unsplash served by Lorem Picsum under the Unsplash licence. List the ids you used in your report; they are meant to be replaced by the project's own pictures. ## 5. Cropping and placing - **Choose a small set of ratios and stick to them:** for example 4:5 for portraits, 16:10 for landscapes and 1:1 for details. Random ratios look like a stock dump. - **Go large.** A photograph at full width, or at half the screen and full height, has presence. Six small ones in a grid have none. If the image is good, give it the room; if it is not, cut it. - **Crop with intent.** Use `object-fit: cover` with an `object-position` chosen per image so the subject sits where the composition needs it (off-centre, on a third, against the text side). - **Let images touch edges.** Full-bleed, or bleeding off one side, reads as designed. An image floating with equal margins on all sides reads as placed by default. - **Overlap sparingly and on purpose:** a headline whose last line runs over the top edge of the picture, a small image overlapping a large one by a fixed 40–80px. One overlap per screen at most. - **Square corners** unless the direction or the one-motif shape says otherwise. If rounded, one radius for every image on the page. - **No frames:** no borders, no shadows, no device mock-ups, no browser chrome around pictures. - **Captions** are one short line in the small size and soft ink under the image, left-aligned to its edge. Most images need none. ## 6. Treatment One treatment for the whole page: - **Untouched.** The default. Pick images whose light already agrees. - **Greyscale.** `filter: grayscale(1) contrast(1.05)`, or `?grayscale` on the URL. Unifies a mixed set instantly and suits editorial and typographic directions. Apply to every image or none. - **Multiply on a field.** On a light flat ground, `mix-blend-mode: multiply` makes a white studio background vanish so a product sits directly on the colour. - **Darkened for a dark page.** `filter: brightness(0.85) contrast(1.05)` so the image edges sink into the ground. Not treatments: colour washes over photographs, duotone overlays, blur, grain overlays, vignettes, tilted "polaroid" frames with shadows. For text on a photograph, a neutral scrim covering only the text area: a solid block at 40–55% black, or a fade from 55% black to transparent over the lower third. Never a coloured overlay. ## 7. Showing software - Build a real fragment of the interface in HTML at its true size, with believable content, instead of a shrunken screenshot or a decorative mock-up. Crop to the part that makes the point: one control, one row, one panel. - Believable means real labels, real numbers that add up, one item hovered or selected, proper alignment. Grey bars standing in for text are worse than no image. - Put the fragment directly on the page or on one flat stage colour. No laptop, no phone frame unless the product is a phone app and the frame is a plain rounded rectangle. - Inside a fragment the product's own interface conventions apply (its small radii, its 1px control borders, a shadow on its open menu). Put the attribute `data-ui` on the fragment's root element: the inspector and the linter then leave what is inside alone, and hold the page around it to the house rules. `data-ui` is for cropped fragments only; wrapping a heading or a whole section in it fails. Write the fragment's CSS under a `[data-ui]` selector (`[data-ui] .row { … }`) so the linter can tell it apart from page styles. - If the user supplies real screenshots, show them large and uncropped at least once. ## 8. Drawing the subject When nothing real can be photographed and the open collections hold no honest picture of it, draw it, and draw it well. Inline SVG and CSS are enough. Drawings and found pictures can share a page: the found ones show the world around the client, the drawings show the client's own things. - **Draw the subject's own things,** not decoration: the stool's three legs and the grain of its seat, the enamel sign over the bakery door, the hut's two windows and its stove pipe, the street plan, the invoice the tool produces, the festival's stage. If you cannot name what a drawing depicts in the subject's world, it is decoration. - **One graphic language for the whole page:** flat filled shapes, no outlines or one consistent stroke weight, the same corner and curve vocabulary everywhere, drawn in the palette's real colours (fields and accent at full strength, not greys). A set of drawings that obviously belong together reads as an identity; a mix of styles reads as clip art. - **Colour is the material.** A product sold on its finish is drawn in that finish's colours; a sea house in the sea's blues and the sand; never a page of grey placeholders. - **Draw with three levels of detail.** Jurors called simple drawings "basic" every time. Give each drawing big shapes that read at a glance, middle shapes that describe the thing (the handle, the window frame, the step), and small details that reward a second look (the maker's mark, the house number, the chipped tile, the hinge, a bird on the roof). Make light with flat tone steps (a lit face and a shaded face of each volume), not gradients. A drawing that would pass as a placeholder icon at full size is not finished. - **Draw large and let it work:** the drawing is the hero's dominant element, a full-width band, a set of tiles, the footer mark. Small doodles scattered around read as filler. - **Let it carry the idea through the page,** the way a motif does: the same drawn object returns at different scales, the tile grid becomes the opening hours, the map becomes the booking section. - **Honesty:** say plainly, in small text near the first drawing or in the footer, that the pictures are drawn until photographs exist, if the client might otherwise be taken to be showing real products. In your report, list which drawings are placeholders for photography. - **Not this:** gradient-shaded 3D-looking blobs, isometric clip art, generic line illustrations of people at laptops, abstract floating shapes, icons in squares. Those are the generated look. ## 9. Type and colour alone This is a legitimate design, not a gap to disguise. Only 7 of the studied sites use no imagery at all, and they hold their own: a median panel score of 7.5 against 7.2 for the whole set. - Make the typography the image: one statement at 10–14vw, a list set at 5vw, numerals at display size. - Use colour at scale: a full field, an inverted section, a two-field split. - Use the subject's own shape as one flat motif if the direction calls for it (a circle, an arc, a notch), drawn in CSS, cropped by the viewport. - Do not add: icons in squares, abstract gradients, dot grids, wave dividers, floating shapes, emoji, generic line illustrations, or an empty box where a picture "will go". ## 10. Markup and credits A found picture, downloaded into the project with `--get`, used as the hero: ```html ``` A dealt photograph further down the page: ```html ``` The credits, as `--credits` prints them, in the footer: ```html

Pictures: “Fig (Ficus carica L.): 57 segments of flowers and fruits”, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

``` - Always `width` and `height` (or `aspect-ratio` in CSS) so nothing jumps while loading. - `loading="lazy"` on everything except the hero image, which gets `fetchpriority="high"`. - `alt` describes the picture in plain words. Decorative repeats get `alt=""`. The script's suggested alt is the archive's title; rewrite it to say what the picture shows. - A coloured `background-color` on the image container (the ground or surface tone) so the layout is whole before the image arrives. - The credit line is part of the footer's design, at full contrast, with its links. Set it at the body size; one step smaller only on a page with plenty of running text, because a long credit line in small type can become the page's most common text size and fail the inspector's body-size check. One line for all pictures; no credit captions laid over the pictures themselves. Credit only the pictures the page still uses. - A broken image fails the inspector. Check every picture in the screenshots. ## 11. Video A moving picture of the subject's world can carry a section the way a photograph does: the river at the end of the street, the roaster's drum turning, a timber frame going up. `assets.mjs --video` searches real footage without keys: Wikimedia Commons (every video there comes with web-sized transcodes; the best source for short clips), the Internet Archive's Prelinger Archives (industrial, educational, city and home films from the 1920s to the 1970s, mostly public domain and mostly long) and NASA (the Earth from orbit, launches, aircraft, laboratories). The rest of the Internet Archive is left out: anyone can upload there, and the licence claims are unchecked. ```bash node /scripts/assets.mjs "coffee roasting" --video node /scripts/assets.mjs "river" --video --source commons,nasa --orientation landscape node /scripts/assets.mjs --get commons:49769620 # the clip, a poster frame, the credit ``` It takes a rendition of 720p or smaller (`--res` changes that), lists short clips first, prints each clip's length and file size, and flags anything over 25 MB or longer than a minute. `--get` refuses a clip over 25 MB unless you pass `--max-mb`, and saves the source's still frame beside it as the poster (Commons and NASA; the archive's own stills are too small). An archive film of ten minutes is too heavy as it stands: trim a few seconds from it with ffmpeg if it is installed, or choose a shorter clip. Licences, credits and honesty work exactly as for pictures (section 3). **Choosing a clip.** - **Short:** 5 to 20 seconds that loop without a visible jump: water, smoke, a turning drum, traffic, leaves, a crowd from far away. Watch it to the end before choosing. - **Light:** under about 5 MB for a section and 10 MB for a hero. 720p is plenty behind type. - **Clean:** no slate, title card, logo, watermark or burned-in caption. NASA and archive films often open with a slate, and the source's poster frame may be that slate. No recognisable person who could be taken for the client's staff or customers. - **Never the client's own:** a found clip of a roastery is not this roastery. - **One per page, two at most.** A page of moving tiles is noise. **On the page.** - Muted, looping, inline, with a poster and a fixed size, as `--get` prints it: ``. No sound and no controls on a decorative loop. `aria-hidden` because it is decoration: whatever the clip says that matters belongs in the text beside it. - The poster shows before the clip plays, on slow connections and under reduced motion, so it must work as a picture on its own. If the source's still is a slate or a blur, take a frame from the clip yourself or use a found picture. - Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, stop it and show the poster: ```html ``` - Crop and place it like a photograph (sections 5 and 6): `object-fit: cover`, one ratio, square corners, no frame, a ground-coloured `background-color` while it loads. - Never under body text. A headline over a clip gets the same neutral scrim as text on a photograph, and nothing lies on top of a headline or a statement. - It is motion: let it be the page's one moving thing, or sit in a section where nothing else moves. - Credit it with the pictures: `--credits` prints one footer line for both ("Pictures and footage:") and the list for the report, with each clip's length.
